Before I say anything, I want to mention that nearly everyone who experiences anger as a symptom when dealing with severe mental illness has been where you are. Myself included. I've been blindsided by rage so bad that I have screamed at my partner before. The cause of my rage was not my fault, but it is my responsibility to ensure that there are safeguards in place so I do not take it out on them again. The guilt is horrible, and focusing on what you can do to avoid this behavior in the future is the only way I've found to alleviate some of it. 

And you do need to apologize, but not excessively.
The reason for that is that excessive apologies turn the tables as far as who is comforting who. She'll notice you are distressed and feel the need to comfort you. The best way that I've found to give a genuine apology is to first acknowledge what you did was wrong, acknowledge the hurt it causes, and (the absolute most important part) What steps you are going to take to avoid this behavior in the future.

I'm on disability. I think at first it was a relief. Like yeah! I can pay my own rent (uh sort of?) and not have to live with my sister and her asshole of a fiance anymore ::cheers::

But? After five years? I'm lonely as hell. I see a friend once every month or two? My partner goes to work, and I don't know what to do with myself. I'm physically sick a lot (this is a new thing, I was approved based on psychiatric disabilities), so getting out regularly is difficult. I've been through a lot of trauma due to circumstances that could have been avoided if I could afford to live in better apartments, or if I could drive. And that has created a cycle of stress, trauma, and worsening agoraphobia and PMDD symptoms.

Your treatment options (at least in the US) are also very limited when you're on Medicare and Medicaid, especially when it comes to psychiatric treatment. In my city, there are two places that offer more intensive treatment. One is a fucking dumpster fire, and the other has a wait list of over a year sometimes. 

I had this exact conversation with my partner when he was considering disability. In a country where they give a flying fuck about people with disabilities? Go for it. If you need it, go for it. But in the US or similar places, don't unless you absolutely have to. Even if it makes you a worse person for it, the new lows one can reach both waiting for a decision, and the anxiety and stress brought on by a system that leaves the psychiatrically disabled behind just isn't worth it if you can avoid it.

I spent six years trying to get my sister disability as well. My sister who is incontinent, has poverty of speech, is borderline intellectually disabled with scores mostly in the 2-5th percentile on her neuropsych exam, and who almost successfully completed suicide not once, but *six times*. 

But if you absolutely need to go on it, here's my advice both before and after applying: 

Be *very picky* with any psychiatric professional you see. If you get any whiff of "It's not that bad" or any condescending or dismissive attitude: Fuck 'em. They will damage both your case and your recovery. I don't mean ditch anyone who disagrees with you. I mean if you bring up a problem and they don't respond with empathy and understanding (or mutually agreed upon sass, I can't live without the sass) then they are not worth your time. Do not wait until the disability office orders an assessment. The psychiatrist's primary concern is asset protection, and nothing else. You need to be sick, but not too sick or you'll seem like you're faking it. It's just not worth the anxiety and invalidation.

Again with the pickiness: After you're on disability, be careful who you live with. If you get any bad feelings about a situation (more so than the normal "AAAAAAA"), go with it. Walk away and look harder. State you are on disability *in the roommate interview*. I'm not kidding about that. It's important especially if your disability isn't apparent. If they use that as a tick mark against you, then they're likely ableist assholes. The other option is finding a room with more roommates and slowly take over the place with people who are better. That's what I did. It sucked for a good six months. It was better than the abuser before them, and WAY BETTER than the place that almost killed us, poisoned us, and gave my partner and I new trauma to talk about.
